title: SRE runtime first-response manual
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a compact first-response manual for on-call SREs to triage common API surface degradations: per-request timeouts, client- or server-side 429 throttles, degraded streaming (broken/choppy SSE/websocket/HTTP2 streams), and spikes in 5xx/4xx error rates. It is intentionally concise — use this during the first 30–60 minutes of an event to stabilize traffic and gather artefacts for later autopsy.

Signal sources and high‑level detection: 
- Alerts: routing-latency-p95 > 1.5x SLO, api-5xx-rate > 2% sustained, stream-disconnect-rate > 0.5% per minute, quota-429-rate > 1%
- Observability: per-route latency histograms, per-backend error breakdown, GPU node health, request queue depth, KV cache hit ratios
- Quick check: Slack #oncall, Redwood Console per-route dashboard, Datadog (or Prometheus + Grafana) overview

Immediate first-response checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Acknowledge in #oncall, assign incident owner (oncall -> lead if > 30m)
2) Mark incident severity and set communication cadence (15m updates for sev2, 5–10m for sev1)
3) Capture core facts: affected endpoints, start time, customer-visible impact, recent deploys/rollouts (Console rollouts tab), infra events (autoscaler, node terminations)
4) Run lightweight triage commands (links below) to snapshot state

Quick triage commands and artifacts to collect: 
- tail last 1k lines of runtime logs for the route (kubectl/stackdriver): runtime-logs --route <name> --since 15m
- query p95/p99 latency by model variant and region for the last 15m
- show current queue depth and worker utilization: runtime-metrics queue-depth, gpu-utilization
- dump recent rollouts and canary traffic percentages from console: console rollouts --recent 1h
Save snapshots to incident ticket and attach links.

Diagnosis heuristics and targeted mitigations: 
A) Timeouts (client sees 504/timeout; high backend tokenization/compile times)
- Common causes: long model initialization, kernel stalls, overloaded queue and high queue-time, backend GC/compaction, large batched requests causing head-of-line blocking
- Fast mitigations: revert recent model or runtime deploy, reduce max batch size or max_latency for affected model, enable synchronous fallback model with lower compute profile, temporarily increase worker concurrency if headroom exists
- Longer-term: add latency SLOs per model variant, add warm-up paths for cold starts, add guardrails to limit request token length allowed to the heavy models

B) 429s (clients receive 429s; quota or admission control enforced)
- Distinguish 429 type: rate-limiter (token bucket) vs admission/queue rejection vs downstream API throttle. Inspect admission-controller logs: admission-rejections by route and principal
- Fast mitigations: raise quota for impacted customer(s) if org-approved, add short retry-after header guidance to clients, activate graceful degrade policy to route to cheaper/compatible model variant, relax some admission-control thresholds for low-risk tiers
- Notes: be conservative changing global quotas — prefer per-customer temporary exceptions and document changes in incident ticket

C) Degraded streaming (broken frames, high reconnect rates, choppy partial responses)
- Common causes: proxy connection churn, kernel-level backpressure, client buffer/timeouts, multiplexing overload on the streaming proxy
- Fast mitigations: shift streaming traffic to a healthy region, reduce parallel streams per worker, increase keepalive and ping intervals on proxy, enable HTTP/1 fallbacks when HTTP/2 shows regression
- Capture: example stream ids, client IPs, server-side stream logs, proxy logs (nginx/envoy), and any broken chunk traces

D) Elevated error rates (5xx spikes)
- Triage: segment errors by error code/stack trace/module (tokenization, shard-fetch, kernel-exec, model-inference, cache-miss)
- If errors isolated to a model: mark model unhealthy, divert traffic, rollback to previous model version, and page model-owner if not already involved
- If errors systemic: consider rolling back recent infra change, scale up dedicated capacity, or flip to global fallback routing policy (route to hosted fallback pool)

Containment vs remediation: 
- Containment is about restoring availability quickly: disable offending model/route, divert traffic to safe fallback, apply temporary per-customer rate-limits, and increase worker pools if autoscaler is lagging.
- Remediation is targeted fix and verifying tests: reproduce, root cause, fix commit, test on canary, staged rollout, postmortem note.

Communication templates (oncall notes):
- Initial post (short): "Investigating elevated error rate for /v1/generate starting ~09:18 UTC. Default fallback routing enabled, canary rollback initiated. Will update in 10m."
- Update (status): "Mitigation applied: diverted 60% traffic to fallback model; 5xx rate reduced from 4.2% -> 0.9% over 8m. Root cause investigation ongoing: focusing on kernel OOMs on gpu-3a."
- Customer guidance: include recommended retry backoff, ETA for full restore, and temporary workarounds (shorter prompts, alternative endpoints)

Runbook action matrix (quick reference):
- If p99 latency spikes: check queue depth -> if > threshold, reduce batch size / increase workers
- If 429s spike: check per-principal throttles -> if single customer, apply temporary quota bump; if global, lower aggressive admission thresholds
- If streaming reconnects high: check proxy latency and keepalive errors -> shift region or reduce parallelism
- If 5xxs from same stacktrace: mark model as unhealthy, divert and rollback

Post-incident steps (to complete within 72 hours):
- Collect artifacts (logs, traces, console snapshots), run regression test suite against suspect models, model owner writeup, SRE root cause analysis, quantify customer impact and cost of mitigation, checklist for automation opportunities (auto-divert rules, improved alerting thresholds)

Open questions / follow-ups (notes to self):
- Should we add an automated circuit breaker that triggers model-diversion after 3 consecutive p99 breaches? (ticket: SRE-742)
- Implement a "stream-health" synthetic to detect streaming regressions pre-prod? (PR referenced above)

Appendix: quick links and commands
- Console rollouts: https://console.redwood.ai/rollouts
- Incident ticket template: confluence:svc-runtime-postmortems-2024
- Common debug scripts: runtime-quick-snapshot, stream-dump, admission-replay

This is a working draft. Keep it terse and practical — add play-specific steps under the relevant section as we learn from future incidents.

Last edited by: Priya Natarajan on 2025-03-05
